The life history of Sucker catfish Euchiloglanis kishinouyei begins with the incubation of small, demersal eggs. The developing embryos are reliant on their yolk reserves until eclosion. Field records indicate that at a controlled water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the entire period from egg fertilisation to the emergence of the prolarva spans approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days]. This incubation duration appears relatively brief when compared to other sisorid catfishes of similar egg size, likely reflecting the energetic demands of the species' fast-flowing montane habitat. Upon hatching, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva has a minimal body mass. Detailed laboratory measurements show that the wet weight immediately following chorion rupture is approximately 0.0335 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0335 grams]. This extraordinarily low neonatal mass is consistent with the small diameter of the fertilised ova, and it necessitates a very rapid onset of exogenous feeding once the yolk reserves are fully consumed.

As the yolk-sac larva transitions into an exogenously feeding pelagic larva, somatic growth proceeds at a notable pace under the cool stream conditions typical of the species. The larval and subsequent juvenile phases culminate in the attainment of sexual maturity, a milestone defined by the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. For E. kishinouyei, this event, known as puberty, is reliably associated with a specific body dimension. Comprehensive sampling of wild populations has established that individuals reach sexual maturation at a total length of 15.4 centimeters [Lp = 15.4 centimeters]. This length threshold is accompanied by a concurrent body mass value. The wet weight at which this life stage transition occurs has been calculated from length-weight regressions to be 36.35 grams [Wwp = 36.35 grams]. These morphometric markers allow for a clear discrimination between immature sub-adults and the reproductively viable adult cohort within the population.

The progression from a sexually mature individual to a full-sized adult involves continued somatic investment until an asymptotic size is approached. For Sucker catfish, the ultimate total length, representing the maximum theoretical size achievable under optimal conditions, is estimated to be 19.3 centimeters [Li = 19.3 centimeters]. This metric is a key descriptor of the species' growth trajectory. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, reflecting the maximum adult body mass, is calculated to be 73.6 grams [Wwi = 73.6 grams]. This value indicates a relatively modest body size compared to other members of the Sisoridae family, many of which are found in larger river systems and can attain considerably greater masses. The comparatively small ultimate size of E. kishinouyei may be an adaptation to the limited carrying capacity and high energetic costs of life in fast, shallow, rocky streams.

Spawning adults of Euchiloglanis kishinouyei exhibit reproductive characteristics that shape the population dynamics of this benthic species. Gravid females are iteroparous, capable of producing multiple batches of eggs over successive breeding seasons. Fecundity per event is modest; females typically release a single clutch of eggs per spawning event. The frequency of these reproductive events appears tied to the annual thermal cycle, with available data suggesting that a reproductively active adult engages in one spawning event per year. This relatively low annual reproductive output contrasts with the high fecundity often observed in cypriniforms that inhabit unpredictable environments, and it aligns instead with a strategy of producing fewer, presumably larger and more robust offspring that are better equipped to survive the demanding conditions of the torrential habitat.

The ultimate boundary of the species' life history is defined by its maximum recorded longevity. Under the stable, cool conditions of their native headwater streams, which average 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum lifespan observed for E. kishinouyei in mark-recapture studies is 4015 days [am = 4015 days] at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to just over 11 years, is notably extended for a fish of its modest body size, which has an ultimate wet weight of only 73.6 grams. This longevity, coupled with the late maturation and low annual fecundity, firmly positions the species within a slow life-history continuum. Such a strategy is typical of species inhabiting stable yet resource-limited environments, where adult survival is highly valued over high fecundity. The physiological mechanisms underpinning this long lifespan, including cellular maintenance and low metabolic rates, represent a promising avenue for future comparative endocrine research within the Sisoridae.
